Headline: Paddling the Twin Cities
Case_study:
Canoe, kayak or paddleboard: Your ultimate guide to paddling routes in the Twin Cities metro area, whether you’re a beginner or a seasoned pro. 

What started as a listicle of places for a quick, happy-hour paddling trip around the Twin Cities quickly evolved into a comprehensive paddling guide, built as a single-page app with custom cartography and stunning drone videography and photography. I served as the primary designer for this project, working alongside our newsroom developer Tom Nehil and cartographer Jake Steinberg (that’s Jake, his dog and I paddling in the video at the top of the page — thankfully it’s muted, or you would hear me gasping each time the canoe wobbled).
![Two adults carry a yellow canoe on land, with a yellow dog in front. ](https://ststatic.stimg.co/assets/outdoors/urban-paddling/secondary/bluffs_secondary.jpg?w=800)
This project was a buffet of piecemeal information waiting to be organized. We started at a whiteboard, listing all the information we needed to show and whether it would be most helpful represented on the map or elsewhere. From there, I moved into wireframing in Figma. 
![A screenshot of a Figma file showing higher-fidelity wireframes](/images/webps/paddling_process2.webp)
I wanted a warm, neutral background and a green accent color to bring the outdoors feel throughout. We added a muted red as a contrasting highlight. The maps were designed to have organic edges, which provide a contrast to the information gridded around them. Gorgeous imagery gathered from the research trips made my job easy, and I made sure each route had a full-bleed photo to provide maximal visual impact and scene-setting. 

This piece was researched and designed in 2024, published in 2025 and updated this June with two new routes. This was a project where I was hands-on from initial concept to final build.

I also turned the paddling guide into a 12-page special section for our print newspaper. This was my second time designing print for the Strib, and I couldn’t ask for a better experience — no hard deadline, full color and no advertising. It was a designer’s dream.
![A newspaper spread showing a photo of kayakers and two maps](/images/webps/paddle_spread.webp)
[You can view the whole paddling print project here.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/annamarieboone/annamarieboone.github.io/master/images/clips/pdfs/paddleguide.pdf)

Headline: Qualls running mate was on Capitol grounds during Jan. 6 attack
Case_study:
My work on this story is a testament to eavesdropping. I was sitting at my desk when I noticed a group discussing something a couple cubicles over — pausing my music led me to help create a scrollytelling hero for a breaking news story about a Republican candidate for governor who attended the Jan. 6 attack at the Capitol.

This piece was turned around in one day.

Headline: What was this unprecedented school year like? We asked the students.
Case_study:
This Minnesota school year began with a school shooting in Minneapolis and ended after Operation Metro Surge. Our education reporters wanted to talk to students about this unprecedented year, allowing them to reflect and process what happened. 

They decided on a video-driven story form, which happened to align with development work I have been doing for a yet-to-be-published piece. I was ecstatic for a chance to use it on a quicker deadline project. I created a visual identity that used a color palette inspired by number two pencils and used a sans serif type that I tracked in slightly to provide more personality.

Headline: Our neighbor, Prince
Case_study:
As a transplant to Minneapolis, I've always been fascinated by the relationship between Prince and the city's residents. For the tenth anniversary of his death, I wanted to gather stories from readers of Prince the neighbor, not just Prince the rock star. 

Readers responded, sending in stories that ranged from the mundane to the truly bizarre. Although it didn’t make it into the final story, my favorite part of this project was getting the chance to interview Prince’s high school music teacher. She remembered him as a shy, talented kid who dressed plainly — something that couldn’t be said for much longer after. 

![A screenshot of eight purple vector illustrations](/images/webps/princestories_process.webp)

I created some lightweight vector illustrations to accompany each submitted story. I translated this story into an [Instagram post](https://www.instagram.com/p/DXhTT7xlXhO/), too.

Headline: Resilience, enlightenment and bed bugs on the Camino de Santiago
Case_study:
For our 30th birthdays, my best friend and I decided to walk 186 miles through Portugal and Spain on the Camino de Santiago. I took fastidious journal entries throughout — no detail was too small to risk being forgotten. I pitched the story to our travel editor before I left, and with his support wrote about our experience when I got back.

It was somehow both magical and mundane, transformative and reaffirming. And yes, we did get bed bugs. At the end of the walk, we each bought a new sweatsuit and threw our backpacks away, unwilling to risk bringing anything home. But despite the bugs (and the blisters, oh man, the *blisters*) I look back with nothing but appreciation.

![Two women stand in front of the Cathedral de Santiago](https://arc.stimg.co/startribunemedia/ZCENIMFP2NCP3OB6PKQXKUOAGQ.jpg?&w=600&h=600&fit=crop&crop=bottom)

My colleague Jake Steinberg hand-drew a map of our route for the story. I brought in my Camino passport, where Claudia and I had to get two stamps a day to prove our pilgrimage, and scanned it to add those along our path. The completed map quickly became my favorite part of the piece.

![a photo of a handdrawn map taped to a white cabinet ](/images/webps/camino_process.webp)

![the same map, colored in with green and yellow and with stamps placed along it ](https://arc.stimg.co/startribunemedia/GIM3CS6XNVEQFAXFNIYGG3IMEY.jpg?&w=900)

Headline: Exclusive! Greatest Minnesota celebrities (of all time) revealed
Case_study:
A joint project I worked on with Bryan Brussee, another designer at the Strib (and a fellow Indiana University alum). Often, lists at the Star Tribune are unordered — from the very beginning, we wanted to lean into the divisiveness by giving readers a chance to vote if they agreed with our critics' selection.

![A screenshot of multiple magazine covers sent as a Slack message](/images/webps/celebs_process.webp)

For the visual identity, we wanted a punchy, tabloid-style look. I pulled photos for each person, adding a paper texture and then doing a rough cutout to look like these were pulled from magazine pages (it gave me a lot of joy to imagine a teenager seeing a picture of Sinclair Lewis in a magazine, clipping it out and hanging it on their wall). I think we did the reference photos and our initial concept justice while still using brand typography and keeping it readable.

Headline: ‘The periodic table for romance’
Case_study: After a lot of heavy work, it was a treat to work on this project from with our Books  editor. I live in the neighborhood of the romance bookstore and am a patron, so it was a natural fit. Visualizing the tropes as atomic illustrations and organizing the tropes into elemental groups was a fun, conceptual challenge.

Headline: A state on edge: What the last 31 days have looked like in Minnesota
Case_study:
A visual retrospective of what the month of January looked like in Minnesota throughout Operation Metro Surge. I had to turn around this project quickly, and to get it published in time I utilized the backend system I created for our [2025 year in photos](https://www.startribune.com/2025-the-year-in-photos/601533059) story. 

I updated the design, using desaturation and blur on the inactive photo to give each day its own emphasis and moment of coming into focus. I also used a heavy cut of our news font for a graphic, type-only hero. I animated the days counting up, which made the month feel longer — accurate to how it felt to live in the cities at this time. I used that same font as an anchor and throughline in the presentation, highlighting each date in the same cut.

Headline: A chaotic confrontation, a gun and 10 shots: The fatal shooting of Alex Pretti
Case_study:
Less than three weeks after Renee Good's death, we were faced with another death of a civilian during Operation Metro Surge. Our nascent visual forensics team reassembled, gathering as many videos as we could from the shooting and assembling another comprehensive timeline. In this instance, there was a lot less movement, so we decided against mapping. Instead, I created highlighted video frames to show how the confrontation escalated. 

There was no break from this news. I drove to work each morning, as early as 6 a.m., and each time saw legal observers with whistles and orange safety vests on each corner outside my neighborhood’s Spanish immersion daycares. When I was coding on deadline on my couch, I heard the whistles as ICE agents were spotted driving through our neighborhood. 

[We discussed the experience of working on these two visual breakdowns for the Star Tribune readers in a livestream.](https://www.startribune.com/live-qa-how-minnesota-star-tribune-journalists-deconstructed-video-of-the-good-pretti-shootings/601576767)

Headline: A close examination of the shooting of Renee Good
Case_study:
The day an ICE agent killed Renee Good, bystander video immediately swept through the community. Different angles fueled different political narratives. During a design team meeting that day, I pitched a visual analysis to break down the videos and create a comprehensive timeline. I learned my colleague Jake Steinberg had begun mapping the relative location of each person. We decided the two ideas belonged together — life during this time was chaotic, and this felt like a chance to provide as much clarity as we could.

Star Tribune videographer Amanda Anderson synced all the clips together, using gunshots to match the video timelines. As a group, we outlined each step of the confrontation to write what we saw. We clearly stated what we could see and what we couldn’t. Our goal was to provide an authoritative source, putting the upsetting videos scattered across social media into context with each other.

I leaned on development skills for a quick-turn custom build that utilized scrollytelling to update the map and play the relevant video clips at each new step. Minutes before we planned to publish, a first-person video from ICE agent Jonathon Ross’ phone was released online. We quickly pivoted, using his video in the timeline to add a greater level of detail and updating the maps and graphics with what we learned through his viewpoint. 

This piece makes me proud to be a local journalist. I am proud of the collaborative work we did in such an accelerated timeline. When the finish line was moved suddenly after two days of nonstop work, I’m proud of us for adapting. The result was the most comprehensive look at the shooting to date. 
[We discussed the experience of working on this visual breakdown for the Star Tribune readers in a livestream.](https://www.startribune.com/live-qa-how-minnesota-star-tribune-journalists-deconstructed-video-of-the-good-pretti-shootings/601576767)

Headline: 2025: The year in photos
Case_study:
We do a photos of the year project each year, and last year I wanted to try and do as much as I could to streamline the process for the years to come. I took stock of what would best serve our team members and editors as we moved forward through the years, and then created an Airtable database for ease of editing for our photo and copy desks. 

I set up clear options in the sheet for selecting galleries versus single images, adding behind-the-lens quotes from our photographers, and more. This was our single-stop editing spot, where captions, photo paths, and even the order of images could be controlled independently of the code. 

To add even more context for readers, I went through our year’s archives to find the original publication story for each photo and included that link so readers could read the original news story, too, if they wished. Even if they didn’t, having the headline for each still provided greater detail and added another layer of information for users.

Headline: Holiday cookie finder
Case_study: I worked with newsroom developer Tom Nehil to redesign the Star Tribune's Holiday Cookie Finder, a database of over 100 different holiday cookie recipes submitted by readers since 2003. We brought in a warm and nostalgic color scheme, as well as a recipe page design directly inspired by cookbooks for ease of use and familiarity. We focused on the print styles, so the recipes could be printed out to a single page and put right into a recipe box. Each year, we continue to update this project as new winning cookies are released.

Headline: Your guide to Twin Cities trail running
Case_study:
Fresh off the success of our paddling guide, the Outdoors team wanted to create another, similar guide for trail running around the Twin Cities metro area. I worked with the same developer and cartographer as the paddling guide, creating a new project that shared visual identity with twists. We used the same color palette and more drone videography as the lead art. At the same time, we differentiated from the original guide — we used different mapping techniques. Because most of our photography was taken by reporters during their runs, we also used the maps as the lead visuals instead of the iPhone pics.

![A black and white dog is wet from a summer storm](https://dgtzuqphqg23d.cloudfront.net/n9EiwBb82B-5a2Ysjfm-_Xj1iB2seWICB5_7lfVLNwU-1536x2048.jpg)

I’m steadier on two feet than on the water. I contributed to this guide, running the Winchell Trail with my dog, Derby. We did get caught in a summer rainstorm, documented above, but would still do it again in a heartbeat. Getting paid to run will always be worth it, and the closest I will ever get to becoming a professional athlete.

Headline: How far can you stretch $100 at the state fair?
Case_study:
The Great Minnesota Get-Together can also be a great strain on the wallet. I wanted to see how far you could make it on only $100. Armed with an iPhone and a dream, I braved the first day, snapping pics up and down every street to collect prices for food, drinks and activities. My camera roll was quickly overwhelmed, and lemonade breaks were crucial. 

![A screenshot of a camera roll with hundreds of photos of signage](/images/webps/under100_process1.webp)
![A screenshot of a camera roll with hundreds of photos of signage](/images/webps/under100_process2.webp)

Back home with only a slight sunburn, I entered all my data into a pre-created Airtable and used those numbers to create a fancy calculator that allowed readers to budget their fair visit ahead of time. This may be the singular project where I learned the most about Svelte in a single go — it really stretched my knowledge and pushed me. I am appreciative of my coworkers who were endlessly patient and answered my repeated questions on deadline. 

I also built in a shareable receipt at the end of the project so users can show off their perfect fair day. This was published the morning of the second day of the fair, giving readers as much time as possible with the updated prices for the year. 

I am excited to build version 2.0 for this year’s fair.

Headline: What's the oldest bar in Minnesota?
Case_study: A story I wrote for [Curious Minnesota](https://www.startribune.com/news-politics/curious-minnesota), our Strib series where we answer reader-submitted questions. As a big fan of good ol’ dive bars, this one was right up my alley. I focused on the longest continually operating dive bar, which led me to three bars in the Twin Cities metro area. I got to visit each, including one that operated through Prohibition through an upstairs speakeasy, complete with a hidden peephole behind a framed photo. There was carpet on the floors, wood paneling on the walls, and Hamm’s on tap — not much more could be asked for.

Headline: An oral history of the six days after George Floyd's murder in Minneapolis
Case_study:
For the fifth anniversary of George Floyd’s murder, we published an oral history of the week after his death. Revisiting this week was familiar — immediately after Floyd’s death in 2020, [I built a visual timeline](https://www2.startribune.com/one-week-that-shook-the-world-george-floyd-s-death-ignited-protests-far-beyond-minneapolis/569930771/) that was part of our staff’s Pulitzer Prize win. 

I believe the best design is always informed by the content, first and foremost. As such, this project is somber, utilizing large-scale photography breaks and balanced typography to allow the story to shine. I knew I wanted to use some of the visual identity from my previous piece, such as a black background and navigation by day. The oral history was a chance to make it stronger, though, and update it with our new brand typography.

I wanted the video to feel integral to the oral history. If readers didn’t enable audio, however, I wanted them to still get the information. I made sure captioning was available and styled the video credits and transcript to be similar to the rest of the oral history, emphasizing its continued importance in the narrative, instead of treating it like an interruption or sidebar to the main text. We edited thoroughly, ensuring the videos and the narrative text didn’t repeat each other.

Headline: Grading the Twin Cities' 52 essential music venues
Case_study: The 53 best essential Minnesota music venues, graded by our professional critics. This story was a personal favorite —  I don't see as many shows as the pros, but I do my best! I added an interactive element for readers so they could keep track of the venues they've been to and share their results with friends and family.

Headline: Ghost of a Chance Podcast
Case_study:
Ghost of a Chance is the Star Tribune's first foray into serialized podcasting. This project was a big undertaking, and one that stretched the capabilities of our newsroom. There were many pieces to this project beyond the landing page — we designed a custom page for each podcast episode with information and additional resources referenced in that episode.

![A screenshot of a Figma file showing multiple page layout options](/images/webps/goac_process.webp)

I also designed discussion guides and printed transcripts, business cards to use for podcast promotion, and helped art direct the podcast cover art, which was illustrated by Brock Kaplan. 

![A newspaper spread showing an obituary for Clementine Robinson](/images/webps/goac_spread1.webp)

![A newspaper spread showing many historical page tears](/images/webps/goac_spread2.webp)

After the final episode, I also designed a special section for our print paper. This was my first time designing a print product for the Star Tribune, and my first time doing print design since 2016. Repurposing an audio story for print was a unique challenge, but I couldn’t have had better team members to help guide me as I reimmersed myself in a dormant medium.

[You can view the whole Ghost of a Chance special section here.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/annamarieboone/annamarieboone.github.io/master/images/clips/pdfs/ghostofachance.pdf)

Headline: Minnesota’s ghost towns are a relic of grand visions gone awry
Case_study: A story I wrote for [Curious Minnesota](https://www.startribune.com/news-politics/curious-minnesota), our Strib series where we answer reader-submitted questions. When I saw this question in the list of story ideas,  I knew I had to take it. Reporting led me to the original ghost town the reader mentioned, Nininger, and to many others throughout the state. History that was just a touch haunted — my favorite.

Headline: Spring arts preview
From one to all
Case_study:
To commemorate the first all-female St. Paul city council, myself, Katie Galioto and Jake Steinberg put together a timeline showing how we got here — starting with the first councilwoman ever elected. 

![Old city council books lined up on a library shelf](/images/webps/stpwomen_process2.webp)

The records were not digitized, so we spent hours in the St. Paul library, reading council meeting notes from the early 1900s and assembling a timeline of how the council changed after Elizabeth Decourcey's election. We plotted everything we found into a spreadsheet, which went through several iterations before we turned it into a scrollytelling graphic.

![a screenshot of a spreadsheet showing a timeline of st paul council members](/images/webps/stpwomen_process.webp)

From there, we dug into the newspaper archives to create biographies of each woman who had served.

Headline: 10 years, 10 couples
Case_study: On Aug. 1, 2013, when the state’s marriage law became gender-neutral, gay, lesbian and nonbinary couples entered into an institution they’d long been denied, claiming its rights and complications. We looked back at 10 years of same-sex marriage in Minnesota by having conversations with 10 couples, nine of whom married — and in one case, divorced — over the decade.

Headline: What surprise songs will Taylor Swift perform in Minneapolis?
What happened to Heather Mayer?
Case_study: Police ruled Heather Mayer’s death a suicide. Her mother set out to prove them wrong and uncovered an escalating tale of violence. Nearly four years later, the circumstances of Heather’s death remain a mystery. This story was reported for years before it was published. As designers, myself and the print designer, Josh Jones, had to balance a careful line between showing the true nature of the abuse and not retraumatizing or being gratuitous. We made careful design choices to give readers control over their experience in the story.

Headline: Life before Roe v. Wade
Case_study: Less than 50 years ago, abortion was illegal in most states. Some Minnesotans remember it well. Anticipating that Roe v. Wade would be in front of the Supreme Court again, reporters asked for stories from people who were alive before Roe. We created this sparsely-designed story, told through vignettes, to allow their memories to shine. Due to the pre-planning, this feature was able to be published at the same time as our live news coverage when Roe was reversed.

Headline: How Twin Cities housing rules keep the metro segregated
Case_study: To examine residential zoning patterns in the Twin Cities, the Star Tribune requested zoning maps from more than 100 communities and reporters reviewed zoning ordinances from each city. The results found that people of color were disproportionately living in multi-family housing due to the racist history of zoning laws.

Headline: Breaking down the video: What happened during Daunte Wright's fatal traffic stop
Case_study: An analysis of the body camera footage with insights from the Brooklyn Center Police policy manual and a comparison of guns and tasers. This story took four days, from initial pitch to publication.

Headline: George Floyd's search for salvation
The siege, evacuation and destruction of a Minneapolis police station
One Week in Minneapolis
Case_study: I was furloughed the Thursday and Friday of Memorial Day weekend. Like so many others, I spent the week refreshing Twitter, seeking constant information as the city reeled after the murder of George Floyd. I pitched this project to my bosses that Friday, and worked over the weekend to collect the best of our Star Tribune coverage and compile it into a visual timeline of the week in Minneapolis that changed the world.

Headline: Best of the Decade
Denied Justice
Case_study: Denied Justice was an investigation into the police handlings of sex assault cases in Minnesota. The Star Tribune team built its own database by requesting records from across the state, and came to the sobering conclusion that only 7% of reported sexual assaults ended in conviction — the majority were never even forwarded to prosecutors. This was a huge undertaking, and in the end resulted in nine stories, a video database, a landing page, and a sister podcast produced with a local television station.
